    AI Overview
    The Pharisees were an influential Jewish social movement and school of thought in Palestine during the Second Temple period (c. 515 BCE–70 CE) known for their strict adherence to both written law and oral tradition. They emphasized personal piety, ritual purity, and believed in the resurrection of the dead, afterlife, and the existence of angels. 
    Core Beliefs and Key Characteristics 
    • Oral Torah: They believed in the binding force of oral tradition, or the "unwritten Torah," alongside the written Mosaic law.
    • Separation: Their name likely derives from the Hebrew Perushim ("separated ones"), referring to their dedication to purity and separation from impurity.
    • Theology:
      They believed in divine providence combined with human free will, the immortality of the soul, and the resurrection.
    • Social Standing: They were often middle-class, popular with the common people, and served as leaders in synagogues.
    • Internal Divisions: Two main schools existed—the strict school of Shammai and the more lenient school of Hillel. 
    Practices and Rituals 
    • Purity Laws: They meticulously applied Levitical purity laws, originally meant for priests, to daily life and meals.
    • Tithing: They were scrupulous about paying tithes and offering, according to JewishEncyclopedia.com.
    • Synagogue Focus: They emphasized study and interpretation of the law, shifting focus away from exclusive reliance on Temple sacrifices. 
    Origin and Legacy 
    • Origin: Emerging during the Second Temple period, they were likely related to the Hasidim (pious ones) who opposed Hellenization in the Maccabean period.
    • Legacy: After the Temple's destruction in 70 AD, Pharisaic beliefs became the foundation of Rabbinic Judaism.
    • New Testament View: While often portrayed as opponents of Jesus due to their legalism and public hypocrisy, some were sympathetic, like Nicodemus, or early followers, such as the Apostle Paul. 
    Key Differences from Other Sects 
    • Vs. Sadducees: Unlike the aristocratic Sadducees, who only accepted the written Torah, the Pharisees accepted oral tradition and believed in the resurrection.
    • Vs. Jesus: The Gospels often show conflict over ritual minutiae, such as fasting and Sabbath, where the Pharisees prioritized outward observance over internal righteousness.

    AI Overview
    The Pharisees were a prominent Second Temple-era Jewish sect known for strict adherence to the Oral and Written Law, legalism, and self-righteousness. They prioritized ritual purity and oral tradition over Temple sacrifices, focusing on public religious displays, criticizing Jesus's ministry, and often appearing hypocritical, prideful, and judgmental. 
    Key Characteristics and Usage Examples
    • Legalism and Oral Tradition:
      They added extensive oral traditions to the Mosaic Law to ensure compliance. Example: They criticized disciples for not washing hands before eating (Mark 7). 
    • Self-Righteousness & Hypocrisy:
      They focused on public piety to be seen, neglecting inner character. Example: Praying loudly on street corners and widening phylacteries to show holiness. 
    • Judgmental Attitude:
      They were quick to criticize those who did not meet their strict standards, especially sinners and tax collectors. Example: Scoffing at Jesus for eating with sinners (Luke 15). 
    • Hostility toward Jesus:
      They frequently challenged Christ's authority, often conspiring with opponents like the Herodians. Example: Plotting to kill Jesus for breaking their traditions. 
    • Rigidity in Religious Observation:
      They placed heavy burdens on people regarding Sabbath laws and purity, often lacking compassion. Example: Criticizing healing on the Sabbath. 
    Synonyms and Descriptive Terms 
    • Legalists: Strict adherence to the letter of the law.
    • Hypocrites: Professing virtues they did not possess.
    • Self-righteous: Believing in their own merit for salvation.
    • Traditionalists: Valuing the Oral Law/Traditions of the Elders.
    • Zealous/Pious: Known for extreme dedication to religious acts.
    • Elitist: Viewed themselves as the true interpreters of the law.

      AI Overview
      In the New Testament, Pharisees functioned as a prominent religious, legalistic, and grassroots, movement focused on strict Torah adherence, acting primarily as Jesus's antagonists through legal disputes over oral tradition, ritual purity, and Sabbath laws. They were legalistic, pious, and, in many cases, supportive of Jesus or in the early church. 
      Key Aspects of the Role of the Pharisees:
      • Theological Opponents:
        They questioned Jesus on his interactions with sinners, ritual purity, and breaking traditional Sabbath rules. 
      • Legalists and Scribes:
        As experts in the Law of Moses, they promoted both the written Torah and a massive body of oral traditions. 
      • Religious Teachers:
        They held significant influence among common people, teaching in synagogues and advocating strict separation from Roman and Hellenistic influences. 
      • Allies and Supporters:
        Some Pharisees were sympathetic, such as Nicodemus (John 3), Joseph of Arimathea (implied), and Gamaliel, who protected the apostles (Acts 5). 
      Usage Examples in the New Testament:
      • Conflict with Jesus: Pharisees question why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 9:11).
      • Sabbath Law Disputes: They confront Jesus for curing people on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1-14).
      • Warning Jesus: Some Pharisees warn Jesus about Herod's plan to kill him (Luke 13:31). 
      • Post-Resurrection: Many, including Saul (Paul), initially persecuted the church, while others (like "believing Pharisees" in Acts 15:5) joined it. 
      Synonyms/Descriptions for the Role of the Pharisees: 
      • "Separated Ones" (translation of Perushim).
      • "Teachers of the Law/Scribes".
      • "Hypocrites" (frequently used by Jesus, Matt 23).
      • "Legalists" or "Traditionalists."
      Common Motifs:
      • The conflict between the "weightier matters" of the law (justice, mercy) and minute, ceremonial legalism. 
      • Their role in the narrative as foils to Jesus's message of grace.

        AI Overview
        The Pharisees were a Second Temple-era Jewish group focused on strict adherence to both the Written Law (Torah) and an "oral tradition," believing that God gave Moses detailed interpretations at Sinai. Core beliefs included the resurrection of the dead, existence of an afterlife with reward/punishment, and personal piety through strict purity laws beyond the Temple. 
        Key core beliefs and characteristics included:
        • Oral Tradition:
          They believed that the Oral Law (later codified in the Talmud) was authoritative, passed down by Moses and binding alongside the written scriptures. 
        • Resurrection and Afterlife:
          Unlike the Sadducees, Pharisees strongly believed in the resurrection of the dead, the existence of angels, and a divine afterlife where righteousness is rewarded. 
        • Widespread Application of Torah:
          They believed laws of purity and holiness should be practiced by all Jews in everyday life, not just by priests in the Temple, thus democratizing religious observance. 
        • Divine Sovereignty & Free Will:
          They maintained a belief in destiny and God's providence, while also advocating for human free will. 
        • Messianic Hope:
          The Pharisees held a strong conviction in the coming of a messiah who would restore the Davidic kingdom. 
        • Synagogue Focus:
          They promoted worship through study and prayer within local communities (synagogues), shifting the focus of Judaism from exclusively sacrificial worship. 
        Their emphasis on strict adherence to the Law led to their popularity with the common people but also drew criticism for potential legalism.

          AI Overview
          Pharisees practiced strict adherence to both written Mosaic law and oral traditions ("traditions of the elders") to achieve daily holiness. Key rituals included detailed handwashing before meals, meticulous tithing of produce, strict Sabbath rules against "work", and frequent fasting. They emphasizedritual purity, often creating impurity barriers via stones vessels. 
          Key Practices and Rituals
          • Oral Law Adherence: Believed in a body of "traditions of the elders" that expanded on the Torah. 
          • Ritual Purity/Handwashing: Imposed detailed cleansing rituals before eating and after returning from the marketplace, including washing hands up to the wrists. 
          • Sabbath Observance: Maintained a complex set of laws regarding what constituted "work" on the Sabbath, such as forbidding carrying burdens or traveling beyond specific distances. 
          • Meticulous Tithing: Tithing to an extreme degree, even on small garden herbs. 
          • Fasting and Prayer: Frequently fasted, notably on Mondays and Thursdays, to show devotion. 
          • Ritual Baths: Built mikvaot (stone pools of water) for purification purposes. 
          • Separation: Attempted to maintain purity by separating themselves from ritual impurity, which often meant avoiding certain people. 
          Usage Examples
          • Handwashing:
            Pharisees criticized Jesus' disciples for not washing their hands according to the tradition before eating. 
          • Sabbath Law:
            They questioned why disciples were plucking grain on the Sabbath, defining it as working. 
          • Tithing:
            They were known to tithe mint, dill, and cumin, focusing on minor laws while sometimes ignoring justice. 
          Synonyms/Related Terms
          • Traditionalists: Due to their reliance on the "traditions of the elders". 
          • Separatists: The name "Pharisee" (Hebrew: Perushim) is derived from this concept. 
          • The Pious/Puritans: Known for their extreme, sometimes performative, acts of piety and holiness. 
          • Keepers of the Oral Law: Adherents to the oral Torah. 
          They differed from the Sadducees, who only adhered to the written Law and oversaw the Temple. The Pharisees' practices often focused on outward appearance to demonstrate their dedication to God.

            Historical Context. What is the historical context of the Pharisees?
            About this result
            Feedback
            An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
            AI Overview
            The Pharisees emerged c. 150–160 BCE during the Intertestamental period, likely arising from the Hasidim ("pious ones") who opposed Hellenization and supported the Maccabean revolt. They were a influential lay-driven Jewish sect focused on Torah obedience, oral tradition, resurrection belief, and purity, becoming prominent during the Second Temple period and surviving its fall in 70 CE. 
            Usage Examples & Historical Context
            • Hellenistic Resistance:
              They grew in response to Hellenistic influence under the Seleucids, aiming to protect Torah observance. 
            • Opposed Sadducees:
              Unlike the aristocratic Sadducees who controlled the Temple, Pharisees were scholars/scribes popular among common people. 
            • New Testament Era:
              Frequently interacted with Jesus regarding ritual purity, Sabbath, and oral law, though some were sympathetic to early Christianity (e.g., Paul, Nicodemus). 
            • Post-70 CE:
              They formed the basis for Rabbinic Judaism, preserving Judaism after the temple's destruction. 
            Synonyms/Related Terms to "Historical Context" 
            • Hellenistic/Maccabean Period: The era of their emergence.
            • Second Temple Period: The context of their influence.
            • Hasidim: Their likely direct predecessors.
            • Legalism: Their focus on strict law adherence.
            • Oral Law/Oral Torah: Their distinct teaching.
            Key Historical Context Images 
            • Second Temple of Jerusalem: The central location of their activity.
            • Synagogues: The community spaces where they taught.
            • Maccabean Revolt: The context of their separation from political rulers.
